fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Men will say, "There is surely a reward for the righteous! There is surely a God who judges the earth!" (Psalm 58:11) After all the heavy lines before it, I think this verse lands on hope. The word you picked is the very one the verse uses.

That's the one, baker. David doesn't dance around it. He says, "No, in your hearts you devise injustice; with your hands you mete out violence on the earth." (Psalm 58:2) Both the hearts and the hands get named.

Yes, baker. David says the cobra "shuts its ears, refusing to hear the tune of the charmer who skillfully weaves his spell." (Psalm 58:4-5) The charmer is skillful, and the cobra still refuses to hear. David sets that picture right beside the wicked's venom.
That's what a cobra does in the movies, friend, so I see the pull. But David's cobra "shuts its ears" and refuses to hear the tune. (Psalm 58:4-5) The tune is playing, and this cobra won't hear it.

Yes, baker. David prays, "May they vanish like water that runs off; when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted." (Psalm 58:7) A blunted arrow is a dull one. He's asking for the wicked's weapons to be dulled.

I think the bow threw you off, friend. David prays, "when they draw the bow, may their arrows be blunted." (Psalm 58:7) So he does ask for it. A blunted arrow is a dull one, and that's what he's asking for.
Right, baker. David prays, "…may they never see the sun." (Psalm 58:8) This is a heavy part of the song. He's asking God to end the wicked's reach.

That's it, baker. The psalm says, "Before your pots can feel the burning thorns—whether green or dry—He will sweep them away." (Psalm 58:9) It's fast. The sweeping comes before the pots feel the thorns.
A warning is a fair guess, friend. But the line says, "There is surely a reward for the righteous!" (Psalm 58:11) This verse turns to the righteous. The word is reward.
